PAPER: Original Article JHSMR Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Retrospective Evaluation of an Antimicrobial Stewardship Program in a Tertiary Care Hospital: A Pharmacist’s Perspective Muhammad Niyas, M.Pharm., Krishnakumar Athavil, M.Pharm., Devarajan Krishnarajan, M.Pharm., Ph.D. Department of Pharmacy Practice, JKKMMRF's-Annai JKK Sampoorani Ammal College of Pharmacy, Komarapalayam, Namakkal, Tamil Nadu 638183, India. Received 18 July 2024 l Revised 6 January 2025 l Accepted 16 January 2025 l Published online 20 May 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) programs by analysing the dose appropriateness, antibiotic consumption, surgical prophylaxis compliance, drug selection, and de-escalation of antibiotic therapy based on culture and sensitivity reports. Material and Methods: A retrospective evaluation of data from medical records and antibiotic consumption in the departments of medicine, surgery, paediatrics, and orthopaedics at a tertiary care hospital from November 2021 to February 2022 was conducted. Through coding, the data entered on the pre-designed proforma were converted into statistical variables. Results: Total overall consumption, daily defined dose, of antibiotics decreased from 412.49 grams (g) to 391.60 g (p-value=0.540, confidence interval [CI]=-10.12–17.08). The percentage of antibiotics prescribed was reduced from 61% to 58%, the average duration of antibiotics per patient was reduced from 4.3 days to 3.7 days, and days of therapy was reduced from 399 to 302 (p-value≤0.001, CI=-465.57–353.24). The time compliance of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis was improved from 95.65% to 99.09% (p-value=0.063, CI=-5.256–0.256). Periodically updated, cumulative hospital antibiogram and antibiotic treatment guidelines were functional, culture and sensitivity-based dosage adjustments were practised in the facility. Conclusion: A well-run AMS program helps hospitals in promoting compliance with antibiotic prescribing guidelines, preventing antimicrobial resistance by decreasing unnecessary antibiotic use. JSON: Name: pharmacist_led_ams_evaluation Title: Retrospective observational analysis of pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship interventions on antibiotic consumption, prescribing appropriateness, and surgical prophylaxis compliance in a tertiary care hospital Short Hypothesis: Implementation of a pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship program in a tertiary care hospital causes a measurable reduction in antibiotic consumption (DDD/100 patient-days and DOT/1,000 patient-days) and average antibiotic duration, and increases surgical prophylaxis time-compliance within four months after implementation compared with the four months before implementation. Related Work: Existing approaches for evaluating antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) rely on retrospective consumption metrics (DDD, DOT), guideline adherence audits, and multidisciplinary stewardship teams with pharmacist participation. Prior evaluations show associations between AMS interventions and reductions in broad-spectrum antibiotic use, surgical prophylaxis optimization, and duration of therapy. Limitations in current approaches include reliance on DDD alone (which poorly represents pediatric and weight-adjusted dosing), short follow-up windows, lack of concurrent controls or interrupted time-series analyses to control temporal confounders, variable microbiology sampling and reporting practices that bias de-escalation measures, inconsistent reporting of renal-dose adjustment interventions, and infrequent disaggregation by clinical service. Many reports also omit clear attribution to specific intervention components (pharmacist dosing adjustment, guideline updates, or cumulative antibiogram dissemination), limiting causal inference and reproducibility. Abstract: Problem: Quantifying the effect of pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) activities on antibiotic consumption, dosing appropriateness, surgical prophylaxis timing, and culture-guided de-escalation is constrained by mixed metrics and confounders. Approach: We propose a retrospective, controlled before–after evaluation using ward-level pharmacy dispensing, patient-level prescriptions, renal function data, and microbiology laboratory results across medicine, surgery, pediatrics, and orthopedics. Main contribution: The design uses paired DDD and DOT analyses, departmental stratification, and interrupted time-series and segmental regression to attribute short-term changes to pharmacist-led AMS practices, including dosage adjustment for creatinine clearance, surgical prophylaxis timing, and culture-driven escalation/de-escalation. Expected outcome: The study will produce direct, quantifiable estimates of reductions in antibiotic consumption and duration, improvements in surgical prophylaxis compliance, and measurable changes in de-escalation/escalation rates attributable to pharmacist-led interventions, while characterizing metric sensitivities (DDD vs DOT) and limitations for future AMS evaluations. Experiments: Datasets: Extract de-identified hospital electronic medical records, pharmacy dispensing logs, and microbiology laboratory records from the tertiary care hospital for two intervals: pre-intervention (4 months immediately prior) and post-intervention (4 months after AMS implementation). Include admissions to medicine, surgery, pediatrics, and orthopedics; include age, sex, admission/discharge dates, ward, ICD-coded diagnoses, all antimicrobial prescriptions (drug, dose, route, start/end dates), serum creatinine and calculated CrCl, surgical procedures with timestamp, and culture results with susceptibilities. Baselines: (1) Pre-intervention period within the same hospital (primary baseline). (2) If available, a matched control hospital without intensified pharmacist-led AMS during the same calendar periods. (3) Sensitivity baseline using the prior year's same months to control seasonal variation. Metrics: Primary—DDD per 100 patient-days (WHO DDD definitions), DOT per 1,000 patient-days, average antibiotic duration per treated patient. Secondary—percentage of admissions receiving any antibiotic, average antibiotics per patient, surgical prophylaxis time-compliance (% prophylaxis given within guideline window), adherence to recommended prophylactic agent, percent of prescriptions with renal-dose adjustments where CrCl<60 mL/min, percent de-escalations within 72 hours of culture result, in-hospital length of stay, 30-day all-cause mortality, and C. difficile incidence. Statistical analysis: Compute aggregated weekly DDD and DOT time series for interrupted time-series (ITS) segmented regression with terms for level and slope changes at intervention point; adjust for autocorrelation and seasonality. Use generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) to compare pre/post patient-level binary outcomes (e.g., timely prophylaxis, de-escalation) with random intercepts for ward and fixed effects for age, sex, Charlson comorbidity index, and COVID-19 status. Use chi-square or Fisher exact tests for categorical comparisons and t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum for continuous variables where appropriate. Comparison/ablation studies: (A) ITS comparing DDD-based vs DOT-based effect size and significance to evaluate metric sensitivity. (B) Subgroup ablation removing renal-dose adjustment interventions from the post-intervention dataset to quantify their contribution to changes in dosing appropriateness and adverse-event proxies. (C) If a control hospital exists, difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis between hospitals. Sample size/power: target dataset size equal to all admissions in the defined periods; conduct post-hoc detectable-effect calculation (e.g., 80% power to detect ≥10% reduction in DOT with alpha=0.05 given observed baseline volumes). Data processing: apply WHO DDD conversion for each agent, compute DOT as sum of calendar days with any systemic antibiotic exposure, stratify analyses by department and age group (pediatrics vs adult). Sensitivity analyses: exclude COVID-19 wards, restrict to culture-positive infections, and run propensity score–matched comparisons for treated vs untreated patients for selected outcomes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Retrospective nonrandomized design limits causal inference; temporal confounders (seasonality, concurrent infection-control changes, COVID-19 waves) may bias ITS or pre-post comparisons. DDD underestimates consumption for paediatric and weight-based dosing; DOT may not capture dose intensity changes. Incomplete or inconsistent documentation of start/stop times, surgical timestamps, CrCl values, or microbiology sampling will introduce measurement error. Microbiology sampling bias (selective cultures) will skew de-escalation/escalation metrics. Small sample sizes in some wards or short post-intervention windows reduce power to detect moderate effects and to observe changes in resistance or clinical outcomes (mortality, C. difficile). Attribution of effects to specific pharmacist actions is limited when multiple AMS components run simultaneously. Generalizability is constrained to tertiary-care settings with similar baseline prescribing patterns and data infrastructure. Data privacy/regulatory constraints may limit availability of linked patient-level covariates required for rigorous adjustment.
